contributions.headingText: Gastroblastoma is a rare, low-grade gastric biphasic epitheliomesenchymal neoplasm with metastatic potential that is composed of epithelial and spindle cells. The tumour arises in the stomach in children and young adults.
2F70.1 & XH4VQ1 Neoplasms of uncertain behaviour of stomach & Gastroblastoma
Gastroblastoma is an intramural gastric tumour, most commonly arising in the antrum, but it may also arise from the gastric body {31871808; 19718790}.

Patients usually present with nonspecific abdominal pain or discomfort, in some cases accompanied by a palpable abdominal mass. Patients may also present with gastrointestinal bleeding and anaemia {31871808; 19718790}. Depending on tumour size and localization, endoscopy may reveal a mass with endoluminal growth with or without ulceration {31871808}. Imaging modalities such as CT and MRI will commonly reveal a mixed solid-cystic mass involving the stomach, with variable compression of adjacent structures {20203230}.

The ages of the reported patients with gastroblastoma from North America, Europe, Asia, and northern Africa have ranged from 9 to 56 years (mean: 24 years, median: 27 years). There appears to be a male predominance, with cases reported in 8 male patients and 4 female patients to date {19718790; 20203230; 22849746; 25031764; 25384293; 28731043; 28822310}.

Gastroblastoma is characterized by a MALAT1::GLI1 fusion, and it has been proposed that this fusion gene probably drives GLI1 oncogenic properties and hedgehog activation. Further evidence in support of the oncogenic properties of the MALAT1::GLI1 fusion gene is its presence in a subset of another gastric tumour, plexiform fibromyxoma {27101025}.

Gastroblastoma manifests as a solid or solid-cystic mass involving gastric wall structures with variable degrees of haemorrhage and mucosal ulceration. It is well demarcated from surrounding tissues and may project intraluminally to form a polypoid mass. The tumour can be as large as 150 mm in maximum dimension {19718790}.

Gastroblastoma has a multinodular growth pattern, with mesenchymal and epithelial components present in variable proportions. Neither component is histologically malignant. The mesenchymal component is composed of bland, uniform, ovoid to spindle cells with pale, clear, or eosinophilic cytoplasm, and it often shows a reticular pattern. The epithelial component may consist of rosettes with eosinophilic secretions, epithelial cords, or solid epithelioid nests, which may be either admixed with mesenchymal elements or well demarcated from them. Mitoses are rare in most cases (with exceptions {19718790; 20203230}), and mitotic counts seem to be unrelated to outcome. Neither the epithelial nor the mesenchymal components display marked atypia or pleomorphism {19718790}.

Immunohistochemistry

The mesenchymal component of gastroblastoma expresses CD10, CD56, and vimentin. The epithelial component expresses cytokeratin (AE1/AE3 and CAM5.2) {31871808}. KIT may rarely be expressed {20203230; 22849746}. Both components show strong and diffuse staining for GLI1 {28731043}. SMA, calretinin, CD34, desmin, and S100 are negative {31871808; 19718790}.

Gastroblastoma is characterized by a recurrent in-frame, oncogenic MALAT1::GLI1 fusion gene, which can be identified with both clinical molecular studies and FISH. This genomic event occurs in both the epithelial and mesenchymal component of the tumour {28731043}. The transcriptome of gastroblastoma is characterized by upregulation of GLI1, a key effector of the hedgehog pathway {20360384; 28731043}.

Essential: gastric origin; biphasic epithelial and spindle cell histopathology; expression of cytokeratin in the epithelial component.

Desirable: demonstration of MALAT1::GLI1 fusion.

Gastroblastoma rarely recurs after partial or subtotal gastrectomy {31871808}. Regional and distant lymph node metastases may occur, as well as distant organ metastases. Deaths attributable to gastroblastoma have not been documented {31871808}.
